utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the Prosecution wants to raise a preliminary matter. Can we do it in open session?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. In private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Private session. We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness, which will be Mr. Clark, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we're ready. And it is Mr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is picked up already by you. May I invite to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Clark. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Clark, you will first be examined by Ms. D'Ascoli, you'll find her to your right.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: John Clark.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Clark, before we continue, I see that you have some papers, documents before you. Could you briefly explain what they are?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, these are various reports which I prepared for the Court from my work in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. I understand these are your reports, correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark. If you wish to refer to them during your testimony, please do so. And if you're referring to them, please let us know what you're referring to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, what is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I'm a forensic pathologist, in other words, a medical doctor specialising in discovering why -- how people die. Until fairly recently I was a full-time practicing forensic pathologist in Scotland. I'm just now about to engage in full-time research. I'm still a forensic pathologist but I'm changing from practical work into a research basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you tell us for how long have you been a forensic pathologist?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: About 28 years probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask both you, Ms. D'Ascoli, but also you, Mr. Clark, to make a short pause between question and answer and answer and question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Can I please have 65 ter 30291 on the screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, you recently provided the OTP with an updated copy of your CV.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the document that will appear on the screen is your updated CV, once we have the document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this CV, 65 ter 30291, as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter number 30291 will be Exhibit P2256.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number, Mr. Registrar, perhaps a bit more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2256, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2256 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, do you recall testifying in the Krstic case on the 30 and 31st of May, 2000, as well as in the Karadzic case on 10 and 11 January, 2012?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes. And please pause after my questions.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Was your testimony true, to the best of your knowledge, when you gave it in those two cases?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions today, would you provide the same answers, in substance?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender the two 65 ter numbers that contain the relevant excerpts from these two cases. So the first is 65 ter 30281. And the second is 65 ter 30282. I would tender them pursuant to Rule 92 ter as public exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One of the usual questions which are put to witnesses is whether they had an opportunity to review the transcript of their previous testimony. Did you have an opportunity to do so, Mr. Clark?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 30281 will be Exhibit P2257. And 65 ter number 30282 will be Exhibit P2258.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2257 and P2258 are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the Chamber's permission I will now briefly summarise Dr. Clark's evidence for the record and for the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. John Clark is a forensic pathologist who worked for the Office of the Prosecutor as the chief pathologist for Bosnia exhumations from 1999 to 2001. Dr. Clark also volunteered for several days as a forensic pathologist for the OTP exhumation projects during the exhumations of 1998. Dr. Clark performed autopsies of victims recovered from mass graves associated with the fall of the Srebrenica enclave. He produced reports in 1999, 2000, and 2001 summarising the results of the postmortem examinations of bodies recovered from Kozluk, Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje, Glogova, Lazete, Ravnice, and Zeleni Jadar. Dr. Clark testifies that nearly all of the victims found in the grave-sites were men. His main conclusions were that the majority of victims were killed by gun-shot wounds. In addition, many of the victims at the Kozluk and Lazete grave-sites were found with hand ligatures and/or blindfolds. And that concludes the summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. D'Ascoli. If you have any further questions for the witness you may put them to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes I do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, can you tell us briefly about your role as chief pathologist in the exhumations in Bosnia between 1998 and 2001?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, I was in charge of the mortuary, so an overall responsibility of recruiting pathologists and other staff there, overseeing their work, in addition to carrying out the routine work myself, and at the end of the season, gathering together all the post-mortem reports, analysing them, summarising the findings and preparing the final reports which I have here.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you. And have you already testified as an expert before this Tribunal in other cases?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. Several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: During your employment at the ICTY, I understand you wrote several reports regarding post-mortem findings on the bodies recovered from these graves. Now, in these reports and in the post-mortem examinations did you follow any standardised protocol or methodology?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: We were carrying out post-mortem examinations done by pathologists who are used to carrying out post-mortem examinations, so there was a basic background in approach to examination of a body, looking at the surroundings of the body, the external examination of a body, the internal examination, et cetera, et cetera. We did have a common protocol, or form, which all pathologists had to complete as they were doing the autopsy. This allowed them to record their findings in a logical way, and was a prompt for looking at various -- various -- various things. It was not prescriptive, however. It was -- it allowed the pathologist to fairly free comment in their work but it meant there was a standard to work to.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark. We will see this in examining some of the autopsy reports for some of these graves. Dr. Clark, you wrote a report on Srebrenica related grave-sites in 1999, 2000, and 2001; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: These reports are extensively discussed in analysing your testimonies in the Krstic and Karadzic cases now in evidence before this Chamber. Sir, did you have an opportunity to review those reports before testifying?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And do you stand by the analysis and conclusions of those reports?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender the Srebrenica-related reports as public exhibits. The first is the 1999 report related to the grave-sites of Kozluk, Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje, and Glogova, and this is marked with 65 ter 04514. And it can be -- was tendered as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 04514 will be Exhibit P2259.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: The second is a 2000 Srebrenica report related to the grave-sites of Lazete, Glogova, and Ravnice, and this is marked with 65 ter 04537 and it can be a public exhibit as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 04537 will be Exhibit P2260.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Finally, the third is the 2001 report related to the grave-sites of Ravnice, Glogova, and Zeleni Jadar. And this is marked with 65 ter 05331.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 05331 will Exhibit P2261, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, did you also write reports for non-Srebrenica related sites?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, several of these.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: In particular, did you write reports related to Paklenik cave, Ivan Polje, and Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And was the process and methodology used to analyse the bodies recovered from these sites the same as described in your Srebrenica-related reports that were just admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review your reports on Paklenik cave, Ivan Polje, and Vlasenica before testifying today?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Do you stand by the analysis and conclusions of the reports?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender, at this stage, these reports that I just mentioned. The first is marked with 65 ter 11029 and is the 2000 report related to Paklenik cave and Ivan Polje. And it can be tendered as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 11029 will be Exhibit P2262, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: There's a supplementary report for -- to this report for the same sites. This is the dated the 30th of September, 2002, and is marked with 65 ter 11030.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 11030 will be Exhibit P2263, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Finally, the third report which is the one related to the Vlasenica grave-site is marked with 65 ter 11032 but this should be under seal for the reason that the report names a witness who has protective measures in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, Mr. Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 11032 will be Exhibit P2264, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2264 is admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: We also have a public redacted version of this report, Your Honours. I could tender it as ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think they have to be filed. They don't have to be admitted. I think it is to be filed but I have to check again exactly what the protocol would be ...

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I remember your instructs were related to witness statement. I don't know if it's the same for a 94 bis report. But in any case we do have a public version ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would accumulate the evidence which doesn't assist the Chamber. The main purpose is that finally the public will be able to see in its redacted form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll -- Ms. D'Ascoli, the Chamber -- it's Monday morning, and the Chamber will -- will review exactly what our guidance on it was and tell you the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, did you also work as a chief pathologist on examination of bodies recovered from the grave-sites of Kevljani, Jama Lisac, Pasinac and Redak?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Was the process of examination of bodies and the methodology used there the same as the process and methodology described in your other pathologist reports?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, again, exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And as well were the difficulties and limitations of the pathology evidence the same as those you described in your other reports?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Were the autopsy reports conducted also for -- yes, sorry. I meant to say, did you participate to any of the autopsy reports conducted for these sites?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry, did I participate? Yeah, I did. I carried out post-mortem examinations, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review the four reports related to Kevljani, Jama Lisac, Pasinac and Redak before testifying?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And do you stand by the analysis and conclusions of the report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can I please have 65 ter 11020 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, now that the report is on the screen, do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. This is the Jama Lisac report.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: If we can go to e-court to page 2 of the English, which I believe is page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, we see that the minimum number of individuals exhumed from this site was 51 individuals, two female and 48 male. Now, can you tell us how the determination of age ranges and gender of the bodies was made?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: As with the bodies of nearly all of the sites that we dealt with, the bodies were largely reduced to skeletons so it was only by looking at the bones that we were able to give an estimation of sex and age. This is possible, it's quite a well established procedure, so on that basis we were able to say for virtually them all whether they were male or female and we were able to give at least an age range, if not -- not the specific age, but the range of ages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might just intervene. Dr. Clark, I see that we mentioning here 51 individuals and can you explain how that came about from two females and 48 males.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to explain that. In one of the individuals, we were unable to say whether this was male or female and this was because of the degree of damage of the bones. The determination of sex is achieved by looking at the shape of the skull and certain features in the pelvis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So that was --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, Dr. Clark, if and when later on, say, DNA analysis would be done on the bodies would that help confirm or -- to confirm or correct the age ranges and the -- the gender of the victims?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, by identifying as an individual person then, yes, that would point to the -- that would be the clearly the correct age. The anthropology age is only an estimate and is not always correct but it's an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now at page 6 of this same report, which is 10 of the B/C/S, we read that the causes of death were gun-shot injuries in 46 cases. Blunt force trauma into two cases, and causes unascertained in three cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now can we please go to e-court page 10 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, if you remember, there are a set of photos attached to this report. And I would ask you to please give us your comments and explain what we see on the screen. For example, this is the first photo attached to the report.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: These are simply photos as examples of the type of injuries that we saw. This is a skull. Which was in fragments which has been glued together again. And from it, we were able to establish that this was a gun-shot injury coming from under the chin. If you follow the arrows coming from under the left side of the -- the jaw up through the face and coming out of the forehead. And we can tell that's the direction because of the shape of the exit hole in the forehead. So this is a typical gun-shot injury from under the jaw, up through the middle of the face and coming out of the forehead.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I believe in one of your previous testimony you mention a phenomenon called beveling, if you can explain us what that is and if is a represented in this photo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, beveling is a -- when a bullet passes through bone -- because bone has a thickness in it -- the side of the bullet hits initially creates a round hole but the side from it -- it comes out the exit side, the hole is wider so you get this sort of V-shaped effect. It's called beveling and if you look at the hole in the forehead, the centre hole there, you can see that the edges shelve out all round and that to us indicates, clearly to us, that this an exit -- an exit shot.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark. Can we please move to the next page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask clarification of one of the previous answers. You were asked about DNA and gender and age. Now I do understand that age is a constant factor in human life, how about age, how does age and DNA match?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: DNA does not identify age. It -- DNA will identify an individual and then it is up to other evidence to point to how old that individual is. So the DNA itself will not point to age.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. And I'm just looking at how it was exactly recorded. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, can you please comment on this second photo now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yeah. This -- this -- this probably appears rather complex to most people this is actually a photograph of the front of this person's face. This was a woman. And probably the most identifiable feature is right in the middle of the picture. You can see the top of the nose. It's the sort of projecting little area coming down right in the middle of the picture is -- is the nose. And if you go up from that you see where the eyebrows would and the forehead. The arrow is pointing to an entrance bullet hole on the right side of her forehead. You can see at least half of a circular hole there and that is a gun-shot entrance -- entrance hole. A lot of the bone round about it has fallen away, and was not recovered. But we can see still an identifiable entrance hole and the bullet came out of the back of the head.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us where this photo is taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And if we go to the next page in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: The photograph was taken in the mortuary after we had examined the bodies and was carefully photographed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you please comment on this third photo now on the screens.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. This is a hip bone the right side of the pelvis of the same -- same woman. And what you see here -- the arrow is pointing to a gun-shot wound. This is slightly different. If you look right in the in the centre of that, you see a green area which looks the shape of a bullet. Right in the centre of this hole. That in fact is the bullet -- the shape of the bullet -- instead of coming through forwards as a round hole it is actually hitting the bone side on and so produces this bullet-shaped defect. As it is coming through the bone, because it is coming out of the screen, it then creates this beveling effect which you can see the wide -- really quite wide shelving as it's coming towards us, so that -- that's what that shows. It's just the top of the hip bone.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, I see another green colour at the bottom of the bone; does that mean anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see -- right at the -- yes, it looks very similar but in fact that is just the way -- it's a hole -- a natural hole in the bone that you're looking through there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we're looking through the green background through it or is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The top one is trauma. The bottom one is natural.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can we please move to the next photo. It's the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Again, Dr. Clark, I would like you to comment about this photo.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: This -- this is different. This is a skull from the side on. You can see the jaw down the bottom and where the arrow is pointing is a general area. There is a hole, there which is not a gun-shot injury this time, but there is lot of fracturing round about, and this is caused by not a gun-shot but by some solid blunt force caused by something heavy hitting the side of the head. And fracturing the skull in many bits. It may look similar to a gun-shot injury but to the practiced eye it is not. It is blunt force.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And could you explain us the differences between an injury caused by gun-shot trauma, and in this case, a blunt force trauma if they're visible on the bones?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: It is really the nature of the fracture lines and the directions they go. And the absence of any beveling on any of the edges, so just various features like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And this will be the last photo that I will show you out of this set. Again, I would ask you to comment on this photo.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Again, this is rather different. This is the ribs on the left side of the chest. The ribs have a big -- a natural curve, and right in the middle of the photograph you'll see black areas on each of the -- of the four ribs. These are healing fractures, so fractures which have occurred probably several days previously which are beginning to heal and the healing process involves tissue and swelling, et cetera, and that's what you're seeing here.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And when you say that these injuries must have occurred some days previously, you mean ante-mortem, before the death of the person, I assume; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, several days before the person died.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender -- the Prosecution tenders at this stage 65 ter 11020, the 2000 report related toot Jama Lisac grave-site, as public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 11020 will be Exhibit P2265, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2265 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can we please have on the screen 65 ter 11019.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, it's -- my report on the Kevljani grave-site.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now at the end of page 1 on the screen we read that the total number of bodies and body parts from the whole Kevljani site was 143 made up of 73 bodies and 70 body parts. Dr. Clark, this distinction between bodies and body parts appears also in other of your reports -- in others of your reports. Can you please explain us the difference or, better, can you explain us the standard or the threshold to classify something as a body versus a body part?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: We regarded as a body any remains in which more of the body was present than -- than was not. To typically -- perhaps somebody -- a remains with -- with the chest and perhaps the legs, we regarded that as a -- as -- as a sort of a trunk and the legs, regarded that as a body, even though the head was perhaps missing. It may alternatively have been a head plus the trunk, but the legs were missing. We still felt that was a substantive body. However, if all we were dealing with was a leg or just a small part of the chest we would call that a body part. It was genuinely quite easy to -- to differentiate the two -- or to decide on the two, sometimes a little difficult, but that's what it was. Essentially there was sort of bulk of the body there, it was a body part -- a body. A body, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And were the body parts included or analysed in the final calculation about causes of death and gun-shot injuries?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Not -- not specifically. I deal with them in each of the reports as a separate issue, but they don't -- they're not included in the main -- the main body of the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now going back to this report of Kevljani one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question. On what basis did you determine whether that leg, isolated leg, was not part of what was found as a body without a leg?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We -- our -- our prime purpose was looking at these bodies for injuries and trauma, et cetera, and we did into the have the -- the time or the facilities to concentrate on identification and putting together the bodies. We knew that would be done by other people at a later stage. Really, for that sort of exercise, you would need a very large room and -- and sort of going round matching up body parts with the bodies. Where it was obvious, perhaps from clothing, et cetera, we -- we would attach it to -- to a body, but, otherwise, we did not concentrate on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was the way in which it was delivered to you. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it was delivered, I take it, in body bags often, and then you would just assume that if it was in a separate body bag it was not part of the body although leg was missing in one of the other bags. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it was mainly on the basis of what was found at the exhumation site.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. They had the best view of the bodies as they lay. Clearly, if they were not happy that an isolated leg belonged to a particular body I think it was wrong of us, in general, to try and associate them. So that's how it was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you could not exclude that some of the 70 body part would have belonged to what you identified as a body in another case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, undoubtedly. I'm sure that some of these body parts -- and, in fact, one of the cases we did after handing the bodies over to other authorities, the Bosnian commission, who had some time to look at these cases, then they informed me of their associations and I -- this is in the Paklenik cave case. And I -- I changed my calculations on the basis of -- of their information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honours, Mr. Clark was referring to the supplementary report now in evidence as P2263.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I'll continue with my questions. So going back to this Kevljani report. Do you remember which type of injuries was found on these bodies?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And if we can please go to e-court page 5 of the English report, and it is page 5 of the B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The injuries which predominated in this site were blunt force injuries rather than gun-shot injuries. So these are injuries caused by either the person striking against something solid or something solid striking the person and breaking a bone, and that predominated in this site. In comparison to nearly all of the other sites in which clear gun-shot injuries predominated and blunt force injuries were much less, here it's the blunt force that was dominant, including healing injuries as well, not just fresh ones but healing ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: We also read in this report that the majority of the Kevljani bodies -- for the majority of these body the cause of death was labelled as unascertained. Can you elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, and of all the sites Kevljani was the one which we had to -- there was so many unascertained. The situation was that a lot of these people, most of these people, did have injuries. They didn't have rib fractures. They did have perhaps skull fractures or some fractures elsewhere, but people don't die because of a broken bone. You die because of other complications of that. So, for instance, somebody with broken ribs would not -- and who survived immediately would not be breathing properly, would be likely to develop pneumonia. That is something that we would not be able to see at post-mortem. If somebody had injuries elsewhere, they might have bleeding inside the abdomen. They might have bleeding inside the head or damage to the brain. Again, in decomposed bodies, we cannot tell that. So we felt on the basis of that, just because you had rib fractures, I could not necessarily say that that was why they died because many people get rib fractures in life and survive quite happily.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecutions tenders at this stage as public exhibits Dr. Clark's reports marked with 65 ter 11019 which is the Kevljani grave-site report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2266, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2266 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders also 65 ter 11027, which is the 2001 report related to the Pasinac cemetery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 11027 will be Exhibit P2267, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, finally, the Redak report which is marked with 65 ter 11028 as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just as a correction, the Pasinac cemetery is 2000 not 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 11028 will be Exhibit P2268, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can I please have on the screen 65 ter 27387.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, is this one of the autopsy reports that you performed at the Kevljani?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, this is a typical final post-mortem report.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you please comment on the summary of the autopsy report.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: The summary is just bringing together the findings so we -- we initially talk about the general state of the body, how complete it was, any identifying features in terms of age, sex, any possessions on -- on the person. Then I talk about the ribs -- the -- the sort of injuries that I found, like fractured ribs. I also have identified a fracture of the bones of his left forearm. And I've commented that these most likely represent what we call defence injuries, in other words, somebody using their arms to protect themselves from blows from some weapon. It's -- naturally to put your arms up, and so they get broken in the process. Similarly there were fractures in the face which could have been direct blows from kicks or from a weapon. But despite all these injuries, I could not necessarily say that they were necessarily fatal and so I had to give the cause of death as unascertained.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Does this illustrate what you were describing with regard to the characteristics of this site in terms of injuries and correlations with the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, the -- by the far the commonest injury were fractures ribs, as you would get -- could get from being struck, by kicked, or -- or beaten by weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can we go to page 16 of this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, can you please explain us what we see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: This is just images of -- of skeletons which I encouraged my fellow pathologists to use just to -- to indicate on the skeleton where the injuries were and it gives a very rapid view. Can you see that I've pointed with arrows to fractures of the left forearm bones. This is on the skeleton on the left-hand side of the screen which is looking from the front, and you -- the arrows are pointing there. There's also an injury to his right hand, and you can see the reverse on the other skeleton which is from the back.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So is this forearm -- would this form be in all autopsy reports from these sites?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: The -- this diagram is available in all the reports and -- and the pathologist would -- would generally colour this in, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And you said it was something you encouraged your fellow pathologists to use.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's a very easy visual way of seeing an injury immediately rather than -- well, it's in addition to the text, but this gives a very immediate image.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time. I have no more than three to five minutes after the break and then I will conclude my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would suggest if it's three to five minutes that we would continue and then that you start your cross-examination after the break, if that is not uncomfortable for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is all right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Can I now have on the screen 65 ter 30308.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, in your previous testimonies and in your pathology exert reports you describe the examinations that were carried out on the body, on the body parts, and the autopsy reports in which all the findings were recorded, so was this process followed for the analysis of the bodies recovered from Jama Lisac, Redak, Pasinac, Kevljani, and Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And did you review all the autopsy reports that were produced by the pathologists working with you at those sites in order to write the overall report for the specific site?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. Every single report.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, in preparation for your testimony today were you asked to review the autopsy reports listed in this chart and make your observations in terms of authenticity of the documents and content as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And were your observations recorded in this chart that we now see on the screens?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And does this chart accurately reflect your observations and comments regarding the documents you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review this chart after -- with your comment?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. And I've indicated that by my initials in the -- column 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can we go to the last page of the chart.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature on this page, Dr. Clark?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, it's mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And, sir, are you willing to answer any additional questions the Defence and the Chamber might have about this chart and the documents commented in there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, the autopsy report just discussed with Dr. Clark was part of this chart, so I will postpone the tendering of the chart and the underlying documents until after cross-examination, after Mr. Stojanovic has had an opportunity to explore it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's accepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Dr. Clark, my final question: Considering the limitations of the pathology evidence explained in your reports, what was the finding that you found in the majority of cases as cause of death?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: The majority of the cases, these people died from gun-shot injuries, often multiple gun-shot injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you very much for answering all my questions, Dr. Clark. I don't have further questions at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I will have to deal with the associated exhibit but we can do it after the break or after the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. D'Ascoli. Judge Fluegge may have one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, only a question to you, Ms. D'Ascoli. You didn't tender the 65 ter 27387.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, I was explaining that that is an autopsy report that is part of chart; therefore, I will postpone it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it's time for a break. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break, and we'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Clark, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor. First of all, I should like to go through your reports so you can clarify some of our dilemmas. And then I would put to you a few specific autopsy reports, again, with some clarifications I thought I'd need when I was reading them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we a see P2259 in e-court, page 1, and -- in English and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, let's use this just as a -- an example. Towards the bottom of this page, in a report for 1999, out of these four graves, Kozluk, Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje, Glogova, you provided a final number for each of the four localities citing complete bodies and body parts found in these graves. You spoke about this in response to a question from the Trial Chamber as to what is considered to be a complete body, speaking of Kevljani. I should like to ask you whether the same criteria were used in your work in cases concerning Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, exactly the same approach was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During your work from 1999 through 2000 or 2001, were any changes made to these criteria determining what is considered to be a complete body and what is concerned -- considered to be a body part? Were there any changes in your methodology?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No, not at all. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This confuses me a little because --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to look at P2261 now, page 10 in English and page 11 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your final report, you state -- you can see that in the bottom part of page 10. It was not easy to decide what should be called body and what should be called body part, even when the latter comprised a large part of the body. Once the mortal remains were cleaned and became visible in the morgue --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel give us a reference to the English text, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the interpreters would like you to give a reference to where you are reading in the page and so also do I need that kind of help. Where are you reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm reading from the final report, which is now P2261, page 10 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be the chapter subheaded, "body parts," in the middle of this page we see in front of us in smaller lettering.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We have found it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So, Professor, from the initial assessment by the field team there was a certain amount of reinterpretation in the mortuary, et cetera, et cetera. From your recent answer, I see a little contradiction with this passage, meaning that in the course of your work, you did modify the initial assessment of the field team that some cases were moved from the category body parts to complete body. What is this all about?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps I misinterpreted your question. I -- I thought you were asking me what was my personal approach in dealing with trying to decide whether a body was a body part or a body. That remained the same throughout the years I was involved. I can see where the confusion lies, because at the start of this report, quite rightly, I list for Kozluk - for instance, this is page 1 of the 1999 Srebrenica site - I list 233 body parts. That is what was presented to us by the field team when they came to the mortuary. We had the benefit in the mortuary of being able to clean up the remains and perhaps find parts of a quite separate body in the body -- in the body bag, which the field team had assumed were one body but in fact clearly could not have been, and we made that into a body part. That is why there's a difference in numbers. But, in terms of my personal approach into deciding these things, that always remained the same. I don't think there's anything contradictory into what -- what the field team found and to what we eventually decided, because we had the advantage of time, space, and cleaning -- cleaning the remains up. And that was the whole purpose of that. So I understand -- I can see why there may be some confusion over it, but there was no conflict between the field team and the mortuary team, but we had the advantage, and that's why I get a different figure in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this text in your final report, you go on to say: "Reviewing for the purposes of this final report all individual autopsy reports, I made further adjustments in re-classified some of the larger body parts into bodies. The original reports will, of course, still have them classified as body parts but the updated re-classification can be provided if required - it involves 23 cases." My question, Professor, would be: Does this digression from your final report impact on any way on the data you provided in this specific report for 1999 Kozluk, Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No. The -- the -- my comments are based on what were finally -- what I finally took to be whole body -- or bodies. I had the advantage, having been there much longer than some of the other pathologists, of having seen far more bodies. And in reviewing the cases, the individual post-mortem reports, I was -- I -- I felt able to say, Well, I think we should probably call this a body, a full body, rather than a body part. I've been very open about that and said that it only involves a small number of cases, but the -- the -- my overall reports are based on that final -- final judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I should like to clear up one dilemma I had during your direct examination. You said earlier today, if I understood this correctly, from the field aspect of the work organisation, field-workers bring in marked bags body parts or complete bodies to the mortuary; and you say, if I understood this correctly, that you did not have the strength, the resources, the time, or the space to assemble body parts to fit the "incomplete bodies," incomplete in quotation marks, because not all the 206 bones that are present in the human body are there. Did I understood this well?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Really, the only way to associated a body part with a body at that time would be just a physical match; in other words, thinking that that bone looks very similar to another one and see if they fit in. Nowadays, of course, that could be done with DNA connecting it and has been done. In 1999, we did not -- that facility did not exist. So if we had attempted to match up every body part with every body, it would have been endless, and I don't think we would have ever finalised it. So we took the decision to concentrate our efforts on what could be -- the information that could be attained from the main bodies and work on that. Otherwise, I think it would -- we would never have got on -- on with the work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Clark, could I ask you the following: Do I understand you well that you say by the DNA analysis, which perhaps was performed later, that the whole issue of what is a body part and what is a body became obsolete because they would be associated through the DNA test anyhow, if there was a DNA test successfully completed on the body part and the body.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm -- I'm -- I'm sure I would be right in saying if we had attempted to put a body part into a body which we thought physically fitted, I'm sure that subsequent DNA testing would say we were wrong in that, in some cases. So I think it would have been an endless exercise for us to try and match them up at that stage. DNA analysis has -- has achieved a lot of reassociation since then. I'm not sure if I answered your question, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, to some extent yes; to some extent, no. I do understand that what is classified as a body part only --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if there is a classified body which would belong to the same person, through DNA testing of the two, that would become apparent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My next question is: You said, Well, when we made -- when we classified a number of bones as one body --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if we would have mixed in a separate bone which did not belong to the body --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you said that that would likely have been found out. But if I have a whole body with -- with, let's say, two or three bones foreign to that body --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- would that be detected? It -- I can imagine that it has got something to do with the DNA sampling from that whole body. You wouldn't take DNA from all the bones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, indeed not. No. You're right. You would have to take a DNA from every single bone and try and match them up which is really quite impossible. We certainly did find in some of our whole bodies extra bones which clearly belonged to somebody else and we would take them out and make them into a body part. Yes, the whole thing is difficult. I think we achieved the best we could at that time, and I think with the bodies there's a substantial number of cases to work with and analyse and -- yes, it would have been interested to fit in the body parts as well, but that couldn't be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I do understand that a later DNA test may have resolved the problem of extra bones with the bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Body parts to the bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it would not have detected, if there are any foreign -- at least there is a risk that you would miss the presence of bones foreign to the body even if you had made a DNA test on the body.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which might also have caused that the extra bones which were joined to the whole body --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- would not have been -- could not be matched to other bodies or other body parts because you would not have taken DNA from that specific small little bone or whatever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Undoubtedly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I think I understood you, more or less.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, why did I ask this? In the mortuary at Visoko as a forensic pathologist, did you also verify and analyse damage to body parts, separate body parts, the bones which could never be matched up to any body? Or to put it more simply, for instance, you have part of a femur where damage is noted that could be subject to your analysis. Did you also analyse that and make an autopsy report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Every single body part was examined. For every single body part a report was produced and I think you will find in the overall reports a separate analysis of the body parts. And identifying that the majority probably had no injuries at all. It was just a forearm or some other limb which had come apart. But some of the body parts were skulls with clear gun-shot injuries or another bone with clear gun-shot injuries. We just noted that, but we did not try and match that into the main -- into the main bodies. But every single body part was looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I've seen that in your reports, but I'm asking you all of this for the following reason: You analysed very meticulously in your report the number of gun-shots to which a body was exposed, and in each summary you concluded from that how many shots a certain body received. Now, if you have done that, and you have not matched body parts - for instance, a forearm that was exposed to one projectile according to an autopsy report - with a body that is perhaps also examined and which you consider according to your methodology as a complete body that was exposed to two gun-shots, how do you then draw the conclusion as to the total number of gun-shots that hit that body if you have not matched them up, the forearm and the body?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, I fully accept what you're saying, and they will be -- in that case, we will have underestimated a number of the gun-shot injuries. I don't think it's a huge number, and I don't think it changes a huge amount of the conclusions I brought. But you're correct, you're entirely correct, that it would underestimate the shots to a particular individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But that notwithstanding, Doctor -- sorry. That notwithstanding, you would still have the number of the projectiles that hit the body --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- and the number that hit the part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I was not able to -- I didn't know that that body part belonged to that body, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That would be the only difference --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be the only difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- that you can't put that part to the body --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- but the injuries you can identify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We can identify the injuries. So if you took overall, forgetting identity, you -- you could get a larger number of overall shots to these people. But as I say, I don't think it affects the overall emphasise a great deal. Most of the body parts did not have injuries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I understand. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a follow-up question just to clarify the matter. If you established cause of death, the person who died because of gun-shot wounds --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- if there would have been more shots and wounds on separate parts of the body that wouldn't change your overall assessment, died by gun-shot wounds; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If there was sufficient fatal injuries in the -- in the -- in the body, shall we say, sufficient to -- as a cause of death I would have given that as a cause of death. It may well be that there was a separate skull which belonged to that body which also had a gun-shot injury, which would also have been a cause of death, but -- but already had a cause of death in the -- in the rest of the body. You -- you will see in the -- and it is cited in the Paklenik cave case that we did, for once, have an opportunity to reassociated some of the body parts into the whole bodies, and, indeed, I did change causes of death in just a few of these cases based on the findings of the body part. But that was really only one case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What was the change in that case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I took the view if somebody has been shot in the head, that is immediately fatal and is inevitably fatal. Somebody who has been -- that would be the thing that would kill them because it would be very quick. So if I had said initially that this person who without a skull had died from gun-shot injuries to the chest that takes just a little bit longer to die, a person to die probably. Now I have the head, and I can say, Well, he died really very quickly because of the head wound, and I -- I would have changed perhaps the cause of death to gun-shot injury to the head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But, nevertheless, died because of gun-shot injuries.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The important -- the important thing -- and I emphasise this in all my reports. It's not so much where the shot was, it is that they died from a gun-shot injury rather than whether it was the head, the chest, whatever. They died from a gun-shot injury. And that's the main important evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That didn't change.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That did not change, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry to make a follow-up. The converse of that argument, Doctor, would be that if the injury to the part was not to the head but to an arm, and you told us a little earlier that an injury to the arm is not going to cause death unless there's excessive bleeding --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- so, in fact, if later it turns out that that arm belongs to the body --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- it doesn't change your determination of the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does not, no. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But could I -- but the unascertained cause of death just on the basis of the body parts after being associated with the skull or whatever would then -- that arm suddenly would have died from bullet --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Bullet wounds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a possibility. In general, if somebody -- the only finding was a gun-shot injury to the arm. We did not classify that as a true cause of death. That was the general principle we took. You could argue that somebody with a gun-shot injury to the arm who was unable to move, who would lose blood, not getting any medical help would eventually die, but we could not definitely prove that, so that was left as unascertained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But once associated with a skull, then you could at least determine that the person --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That had been shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that had been shot --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even if on the basis of just the arm, you couldn't determine any cause of death because it might just have caused a fracture and not a fatal bleeding, for example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly. But if that was the only injury on the body, just the arm, yes, it indicates that he's been shot. But we would probably still have given the cause of death as unascertained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in view of your many years of experience as a pathologist could you agree with me in principle that a shot or several shots in one body would indicate that this is random firing at that body rather than precise targeting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I don't think that's true. You could target somebody with four or five shots, one after the other, that's still a target. So I don't think that takes -- takes -- takes away from it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And it works the other way around. One shot with a lethal outcome, could it, in principle, indicate proximity between the weapon and the late person? Would that indicate precise firing or targeting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Not necessarily, no. That could be a single shot, could be a random -- so-called, random shot to a person, or it could be targeted, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it has got nothing to do with the distance, if I understand you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like us to look at P2259 in e-court, please; page 2, both in English and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, this is your report for 1999. I would just like us to take a look at one particular section. The last paragraph on this page. You are commenting upon autopsy reports, and you say: "The overall structure of each report may have been similar but the descriptive style and the form of words used varied considerably from pathologist to pathologist, not least reflecting the ease of use of the English language and the different medico-legal backgrounds from which each of them came." This is what I'm asking you now: These words of your here -- different medico-legal backgrounds from all of them or of all of them, did this contribute to your overall task and that is ascertaining the cause of death, if I understand things correctly?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No. These pathologists may have come from different countries, different backgrounds but they were all pathologists. So they all worked on the same principle of examination of a body, to look for findings and determine cause of death. It was my task -- I mean, inevitably and you have this with lawyers, with anybody, different people of a profession will describe things slightly different. Somebody will use more words than another one and so we had this with the pathologists. It was my job afterwards to, in reviewing all these cases, to just to pick out what -- what they were actually meaning and analyse that information. But everybody was working to the same overall protocol, if you like, trying to achieve the same amount of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one follow-up question here as well. We see the form of words used, do I understand that you're referring to the phrasing of the findings? Is that what you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. For instance, I found I had -- I had German pathologists. They tended to be very descriptive in their particular -- of an injury. Pathologists from other countries would summarise more, perhaps not use so many, quite so many, technical terms, but in the end, they were both describing a gun-shot injury. We also had photographic proof of that that I could review. We also had the diagrams that they had indicated, so from all that information, I was still able to achieve -- to interpret the overall meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you said -- you referred to the ease of the use of the English language and the different medico-legal backgrounds. Could you explain the -- is that what you just described and was the use of the English language more technical use of language or how should I understand the two categories you mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is more -- I mean, if all the pathologists spoke English, some clearly better than others, so as with any translation, little words are missed out and perhaps a slightly wrong word would be used. But I think I had the benefit, I knew what they were trying to say. When I talk about different medico-legal backgrounds, I suspect that some pathologists in their country are perhaps obliged to put more detail about a particular thing in than, say, in other country, but everyone, all the pathologists at least put all the basic information which was required there. And, as I say, we had the additional benefit of the photographs and diagrams, so from all that, I was able to interpret the findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At one point in time, Professor, at the mortuary in Visoko, you had up to 16 pathologists and other staff working on that project. Would that be an approximately accurate number? Also, they all came from different countries, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: If I could just clarify. The -- at any one time, so for any one day in the mortuary there would be a maximum of three pathologists, myself and two others. I was there all the time. The other pathologists would come for two-week periods -- two, three-week periods, they would rotate. In the whole season we might have about 18 different pathologists. There were other staff anthropologists, photographers, other people. So, all in all, in a particular day in the mortuary, yes, there might be up to 16 people. Three pathologists and all the other people as well. Yes, you're right, they did come from all different countries and that was a deliberate ploy to engage as many countries as possible, not just from Europe, but from other continents, and I think that added greatly to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to skip something and then I'm going to ask you something else and then I'll get back to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I'd like the same document, P2292 [as interpreted], but I would like to ask for page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And then you're going to see the last paragraph, Professor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you repeat the exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P2259. 2259. That is the document that we're dealing with right now, from 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, please take a look at what you said here, in relation to the questions that were put to you right now: "Problems arose, however, where the only findings were gun-shot injuries to the legs or arms. Some wounds to the thighs could well have damaged sufficiently large blood vessels to cause fatal haemorrhage. But, generally, gun-shot injuries to the limbs would normally be survivable." And then the last sentence that I would like to us clarify. You say: "Unfortunately, this could not be proved or even implied. In the absence of any other obvious findings therefore, the cause of death in these cases was usually given as unascertained?" This is what I'm asking you now, Professor: In the methodology of your work, three pathologists or two pathologists working in the mortuary, you're the person who represents continuity, if you will. Who is the person who says what the cause of death is in that report? The pathologist working on it, or you who supervises it, if you will, in a case like this, when there was an injury to the limbs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: It was always the pathologist, individual pathologist, who decided on his or her cause of death. In perhaps difficult cases, we would consult together, because we are working physically very close to each other. We would discuss findings. They would seek my advice, and in the vast majority of cases, I think, we came to a mutual decision. In the end, if they stuck very strongly to one opinion, that was their report, and -- and they -- they gave that. I don't recall that happening, but that would have been the principle. In no way did I -- I -- I might advise or suggest, on the basis of my experience, but it was no more than that. And I -- I did not force anybody to -- I think -- I think if you look at the individual post-mortem reports you'll see quite a lot of variation in some of the wording of, say, gun-shot injury. Some people would call it ballistic trauma or some people would call it multiple fire-arms or something. It all, in the end, means a gun-shot injury but the very fact that they are using different terminology shows their independence and that I'm not forcing a particular form of words on any of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask there a follow-up question as well. Was there any disagreement among you and the colleagues, the other two pathologists, about the standards to be applied, for example -- and that was the example that a bullet wound to a limb would not justify the determination of the cause of death if there was nothing else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no strong disagreement on that at all. We might -- some might say, well -- well, they would argue the same principles that I did: That somebody with a gun-shot injury of a limb, if they did not get any medical help, were left, would inevitably die. And I think we all agreed on that. But we could not give a specific cause. They were entirely happy with the overall approach that we took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You could not speculate on whether they got any medical help, yes or no, and therefore it remained undetermined.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly. And we had to set a line somewhere and I think that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just on that point, Doctor. Did the remains that you were examining completely skeletonize or did they have tissue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From all these sites the majority of people were reduced to a skeleton. In some sites there was, remarkably, quite a lot of tissue on, still, some the bodies. The tissue didn't really help a great deal. Because even though there's tissue there it is decomposed, it's difficult to see anything, bruising or bleeding, et cetera. So, really, all our focus was on damage to the bones --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Skeletons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And of course the skeletons can't show you whether the injury would have caused death because of -- can't see whether it was on a particular blood vessel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly. Exactly, because it doesn't show, you know, your heart, or your lungs, et cetera. All it shows is the bullet-hole in the rib which lies over the heart but doesn't show any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I am going to move ahead in this same report now so that we see whether what you said a moment ago is opposite to what you say in the text. So we're dealing with the same document but we need page 10 in B/C/S or, rather, 11 in English. That's your report again. Professor, this is what you say precisely as you were commenting upon this method of ascertaining the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's the middle of the page, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you say what to include in the cause of death was very much a subjective one for each pathologist. Some choosing to include most or all of the injuries present, multiple gun-shot injuries, others restricting the cause to what was considered the principle and necessarily fatal one, even though additional injuries were present elsewhere? And then you say: "Certain pathologists were also more willing to regard a particular injury as fatal. Others preferring to leave the cause of death, in these cases, as unascertained." This is what I'm asking you now: This wording that you provided here, does it mean that the approach to that final conclusion - and now I'm going to give you an example of that - ascertaining the cause of death was different in the case of different pathologists. Some people were more rigid; others were more liberal in giving a final assessment as to what the cause of death was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, I take your point. It may appear contradictory. This really only applies to a relatively small number of -- of cases.
