I can think it's perhaps somebody with -- where the only finding was, perhaps a gun-shot injury in the pelvis, for instance, my own view would be that that would be likely to be -- very likely to be a fatal injury. Sometimes a pathologist would -- would be less happy at that and would give that as unascertained, and I went along with that. It only -- it was only if a few -- I mean, I would have to go through all the files but I can think it was only in a few cases that that ever occurred. I think I would just -- I'm just trying to emphasise this was not me, although I was in charge of the mortuary, this was not me dictating what was -- what the pathologists were deciding. I was trying to make very clear that these were individual professionals who took their own decisions. Yes, there may be some contradiction in the words there, and I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say a few, we are in this report talking about well over 400 bodies, I'm not talking about the body parts. Could you give us an impression on those 450 bodies, how often would it happen that there was some disagreement about how to interpret what was found on the bones as indications for a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can imagine three or four times or a very small number of cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So 1 per cent --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1, 2 per cent, perhaps. It was small. The bulk of the unascertained ones were unascertained for -- for other reasons, perhaps there was no injuries at all or it was very minor injuries. So it's a small number of cases, and ... as I said, I can think of no instance in which there was any violent disagreements in the mortuary or anything of that sort at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, could we please take a look at one of these reports now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please have 1D01287 in e-court. 1D01287. The first page, please. Professor, I assume that this is one of your reports.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It has an attachment too, but I would like us to focus on this first page briefly. If my colleagues have interpreted this properly for me, my understanding is that your analysis focussed on a body that consisted of a left leg, pelvic bones, and bones from both feet, as is stated here. And then, in the second paragraph, you say that there is -- that there are two gun-shot injuries to the left leg, one to the knee and the other to the lower leg. And then you say, in the final report, at the end of this first page, rather, that you cannot determine the cause of death or, rather, that it remains unascertained. Do you see all of that, Professor?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Indeed yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Does that mean, to us who know very little anatomy, two shots in the left leg, and the knee, and the bone below the knee does not provide enough information for, objectively, scientifically ascertaining the cause of death and that led you to give this ultimate finding?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. Gun-shot injuries to the lower leg would not be inevitably fatal. So, in contrast to a gun-shot wound going through the head or in the front of the chest - I think we could safely say that that would be fatal - so, because all I found was two injuries on the left leg, the lower leg, I felt I didn't really know the precise cause of death of -- of this -- this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like us to take a look at a similar report, 1D01286. On the basis of this report, and it was done by your colleague, a pathologist from Sri Lanka, as far as I could see, from the final report.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It is established here, Professor, that this body consisted of the skull, some bones of the vertebral column, ribs, and limb bones. There are further documents here related to the body parts that were found. Also, it is established that there was an injury to the left leg that came from the back. This pathologist establishes as the cause of death: Penetrating bullet injury of the left thigh. First of all, as a -- for a pathologist, rather, would it be right to say that these are similar injuries of body parts, if we look at the previous report and this report?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: At first glance, it may be. The injury here was higher up in the leg, and there are larger blood vessels to damage. Yes, this is -- okay, this is an example of where there was a slight difference in interpretation. This is a very experienced pathologists from Sri Lanka who has a lot of experience of gun-shot injuries. He has chosen to give the cause of death here. You're right, in the previous one, which is a slightly different injury, I chose not to. That's professional judgement. I mean, I have to say -- that you're -- that these are focussing on -- you're correctly pointing out the difference but overall a very number of cases that this applies to. But, yes, I accept what you're saying, and this is a -- demonstrating slightly different professional judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Given that determination by this pathologist what you did make of the sentence that says: "However in the absence of the skull, some other parts of the skeletal system, and soft tissues whether he had died due to some other injury cannot be excluded."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What he's saying here is that there's at least a minimum cause of death. If this skull had been present and had shown a gun-shot injury he almost certainly would have said gun-shot injury to the skull or to the head, as the cause of death. But he is saying even without that, at least we have a gun-shot injury. Which comes back to the overall -- my earlier comment that the significance is not particularly where the bullet was. It's the fact that they were shot at all which -- which is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one follow-up question. But, before we do so, could we have on our screens in English page 13 of this report. Where you said higher up in the leg, my layman's eye would tell me that it was just above of the knee.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I take the point, and I think almost as soon as I said that sentence, I realised that it was probably -- it's not that much higher up, it is just slightly higher than the knee. It doesn't take away from my comments that this pathologist has taken that judgement. I might have taken a slightly different one. That's -- that's what happens professionally. It's -- it's only -- I stress, a very small -- really a relatively small number of cases that this -- that these disputes ever arose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This would be within the 1 or 2 per cent that you mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic. I'm also -- I'm looking at the clock. Perhaps we should not proceed at this moment. Could you give us an indication on whether you're on track and how much more time you would still need. I am aware that the Judges have -- well, not stolen but at least taken some of the time. Can you tell us at least where we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I believe that I'm on track, that I'm going take the two and a half hours I said I would. So another hour and 15, 20 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While the witness is brought into the courtroom, Ms. D'Ascoli, I draw your attention to the transcript of Tuesday, the 21st of August, 2012, page 12085 [sic] for the guidance we gave at the time in relation to the -- what to do with public redacted versions of documents which are, as a whole or in part, confidential. If that would change, we might have to look at that again. Then we'll certainly let the parties know.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sure. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, before the break, we dealt with the criteria for establishing completeness of a body, the way to determine the number of gun-shots to which the body was exposed, the cause of death. And the fourth subject I would like to broach now is one that we find it in every analysis that you have made and that is post-mortem injuries. Let me ask you: Is it correct to conclude that you as a pathologist were not able to determine whether injuries were sustained before or after death?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, that is strictly -- strictly correct, in the sense that what we were dealing with, by and large, was a skeleton with bone and that did not allow us to say absolutely categorically that an injury occurred before or after death.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: An additional problem in your work was the fact that you had information that some of the graves had been tampered with, attacked, and relocated, and that mortal remains were exposed to possible fractures and damage during relocation. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we were very well aware of that, and we took into consideration in all our findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say, Mr. Stojanovic, that graves were attacked? You're quoted here as having said "that some of the graves had been tampered with, attacked, and relocated." And I'm asking whether you are saying that the graves were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. In the same sense, the word can mean "damaged," "affected." Different terms I used for violated the graves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, looking strictly at your science, where there is no soft tissue, all injuries to the skeletal remains do not provide sufficient information as to whether injuries occurred before or after death.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. If these are fresh injuries, in other words, before there is any chance to have any healing process on the bones, you're correct, that it becomes almost impossible to say that a fracture occurred just before death or occurred after death -- just after death.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where soft tissue is present, or where remnants of soft tissue are present, from the viewpoint of your expertise, would it be possible to determine the cause of death and injuries to the skeleton before or after death?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Soft tissue does help. And clearly in a fresh body, that's what we're looking at. We're looking at the bruising, the swelling, and the bleeding, which indicates to us something in life. Even in -- even when tissues were present, however, in these cases, the tissues were discoloured and any bruising or swelling was still extremely difficult to see. Only in very occasional cases did we see signs of what we interpret as internal bleeding inside the body, perhaps in the skull or the chest, which clearly happened in life, and that -- that did assess us -- assist us, yes. But generally the soft tissues didn't help a great deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you can recall, Professor, would you tell us from which grave-site you had bodies or body parts complete with remnants of soft tissue?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I -- as I recall, I think the Lazete grave-sites had a surprising amount of soft tissue remaining on the bodies. The bodies from Kozluk, some had soft tissues; some didn't. The majority of the other sites, I think, had -- were either completely reduced as skeleton or just had a little bit of tissue -- of tissue on them. But, Lazete, as I recall, had -- to our minds, got a surprising amount of soft tissue remaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Why am I asking you this, if you can assist us. Could that fact, according to the rules of your profession, help us determine the cause of death for that body, or body part?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: The -- yes. The presence of soft tissues can help -- can help sometimes, in the sense as I've already explained. There may be signs of bleeding inside. Also, the soft tissues may trap a bullet there. Now, if the soft tissues trap a bullet, that's a good indication that the person has been shot. But other than that, the sort tissues didn't -- didn't help -- didn't help a great deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For the piece of evidence that I will present to you now, if you can assist us, I only want you to tell me: Am I correct in thinking that if a body is exposed to atmospheric conditions is not buried as opposed to a body that is buried and taking into account the composition of the soil because we've had occasion to hear evidence from an anthropologist as well, would that process proceed quicker or slower, the decomposition of soft tissue?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: The decomposition would be slower if the body is buried. So a body that's left out on the open would decompose more quickly, because it's exposed to air, animal interference, and it -- it -- it would break down more -- more quickly. A body buried in the soil is cooled down for a start. No air gets to it, no bacteria -- or less bacteria. So it takes longer. It will eventually degenerate, but the process will be slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at 1D01289 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for it to be uploaded, it's a letter that we received from the Office of the Prosecutor in the process of disclosure, that one of your colleagues, Professor Moore, from the Association of Doctors for Human Rights, sent to Defence counsel in another case, presenting his experience in his field-work during excavations and disposal of the body, precisely at the grave-site you just mentioned, Lazete, where you said there was a surprising amount of soft tissue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at page 2, item 2, the last paragraph. At one point, we will move on to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But let me ask you first: Do you know Professor Snow and Dr. Moore, because they worked, as far as I can see, two years prior to you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I don't know either of them, no. What I do -- if I can put it in perspective, I was aware that we did the Lazete grave post-mortems in 2000. This was what we determined as Lazete 2. I think I've got that right. But we also did the remains of this grave that I think you're alluding to here. There were some body parts left behind from this excavation that we -- that we also looked at. So my findings on Lazete are largely to do with a different grave from what was being worked on here. But to answer your question direct: I don't know either of these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right, Professor. That's the way I understood it. But I decided to ask this question because in the final report -- at least that's what I call it, that's the report P2260, the report of the chief pathologist, P2260. And if we could just look at its first page before returning to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I apologise, Your Honours, from jumping from subject to subject but we need to clear this up. That's the report for 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 1, this is precisely what you deal with. You can see it here now. You say that the subject of that report is the Lazete grave; you are right. There is a Lazete 1 and 2. And you say - Your Honours, that's the second paragraph after the enumeration - one of the graves at Lazete, Lazete 2, had been excavated previously in 1996 while at Glogova another grave at this site had been worked on in 1999. And you say: "The pathology findings in both have been reported on previously." And further below, you cite the final numbers for Lazete 1 and Lazete 2. So would my reasoning be correct if I said, Yes, what you say is right, by precisely this information from Lazete 2 that was excavated in 1996 was dealt by you in this report by the chief pathologist from February 2001; is that correct? To avoid confusion.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No. No, sorry. No, the earlier examination of Lazete 2, I've never seen that report, and it's certainly not included here. The bodies that I describe in Lazete 2 here are those that were left behind from that exhumation that we did. But I've never seen the original report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. We have cleared that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we can come back to the document 1D01289. Page 2, please, the last passage straddling page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this letter to the lawyers, Dr. Moore states: "The removal of the remains," and he speaking about Lazete 2, "went very fast, almost too fast; for, in some cases not all of the skeletal remains (hands and feet, for example) that went with the person being removed did not get into the right body bag because of crowding within the burials (some parts have fallen off during decomposition. This may account for the non-associated hands and feet as well) as other skeletal elements that were recovered later in the excavation. I agree with C. C. Snow that, on a good day, only 20 bodies should be removed at a time." Now let me ask you, Professor, working on this project, in the mortuary not in the field, did you receive such samples and were you familiar with such situations during field work? With your permission, he also says further below: "Of course, in hindsight, this contributed to the future problem of determining the minimum number of individuals present in the grave." The minimum of individuals. We discussed this with Professor Baraybar. Is your experience similar to his?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: This was a different team who was doing the original exhumation. I understood -- well, I was -- got the impression that our -- that ICTY team were doing a very methodical job, possibly learning from lessons in the past, because this first one, the PHR exhumation, was one of the very first exhumations. And, as we all do, we learn from experience so year by year. But I was not -- I had no impression at all that the ICTY team in 2000 were in any way rushing to -- to get the bodies out. And I got no -- no -- no sense that -- that -- that they'd been careless and that wrong bodies were being put together, et cetera. I don't know if that answers your question or not, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Professor. But it was my understanding that you confirmed in your previous answers that there had been such situations, where you received a complete body from the field, and then, in your work in the mortuary, you would establish that some of the body parts, or some of the bones do not correspond to that body. Or, conversely, that in some other body bags, you would find body parts that the field pathologists and anthropologists had not match up with a body that you called a complete body. Were such omissions the result of human error, or the speed of their work?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No. I certainly did not get the impression it was the speed of their work. The letter that you -- that's on the screen here clearly is blaming the speed of -- speed of work, as I read through it. That did not apply, as I understand it, with the ICTY team. Yes, it was inevitable that bits of bodies would -- would still get mixed up even going at a much slower speed. That's the nature of -- of a mass grave. But that was not the final decision at this field because they still had the stage of the mortuary to go in which we could take even more time to try and sort things out. So I don't think the field teams, any -- any issues with reassociation was anything to do with very rapid speed of getting the bodies out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to look at one more paragraph and ask for your comment. Page 4 of this document, please. We should focus on the end of the first paragraph on page 4 where we can read: "Not to do this, I believe is what Dr. Snow meant by sloppy science. This is reflected in questions concerning, co-mingling of the remains, clothing that was discarded, the determination of MN1, the cause of death, manner of death, and the OTP's review of reports, which in itself is improper; for the ultimate responsibility for these reports are in the purview of the forensic scientist or principal investigator." Did you have knowledge at the time that the work on these grave-sites involved situations where forensic evidence had been rejected as irrelevant, insignificant, or unnecessary?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I'd no specific knowledge. I was aware that there had been difficulties with earlier exhumations and examinations that had been -- there were some dissatisfactions. So all the more reason that in our own work we did not rush anything, took lots of time, and, even more so, I was very conscious of the fact that the chief pathologist should not be dictating causes of death to other pathologists. I think we discussed that earlier because that had been an implication from previous work. So our -- our work was certainly not rushed at all, and I think we got good answers in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we admit all three documents that I used now: 1D20187 [as interpreted], 1D01286, and 1D01289.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. 65 ter number 1D20187 [sic] will be Exhibit D369; 65 ter 1D1286 will be Exhibit D370; and 65 ter 1D1289 will be Exhibit D371.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The first number is wrongly recorded. The 65 ter number should be "1D1287."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D369, D370, and D371 are admitted into evidence. I immediately add to that, Mr. Stojanovic, that the witness said that he was not familiar with what happened at the time although he had heard about it. It was not the practice that he experienced, but since the Prosecution did not oppose, it is more or less from the bar table, I would say, that there had been quarrels before which, of course, we know already from some other parts of the evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, could you tell us a few words now about your work. It is my understanding that you worked on several thousand post-mortem reports, autopsy reports, during those two years of working for the international Tribunal. Would that figure be about right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I think if you -- including the reports from the other pathologists, that's right. I think it's about -- over 3.000 reports that I have reviewed. Yes, that's correct. That includes body parts, of course. But it's well over 3.000 reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. That was my next question. And I'd like to use some evidence here. Could you give the Court an assessment regarding these approximately 3.000 analyses of yours. How many analyses had to do with injures on one bone or several bones? So not the entire body, not the complete body, not a body part that consists of several bones but one bone.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I -- I don't know the exact figure, but there was certainly a number of these cases in which it was an isolated bone was found, and I would do a report on that. If I said 50, 60, it might be around about that. I can't remember precisely. But there were some, you're right, in which it was just an individual bone. It's still a body part, so it had to be looked at and reported on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was told by the people who prepared what I'm asking about today that there were several hundred reports like that. Because I must admit, in all certainty, that I didn't manage to count all of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you refer to your source, Mr. Stojanovic, could you tell us what they are? Is it the people who prepared what you are asking, have they any personal knowledge about -- happened -- what happened there or did they analyse the reports? It's rather unclear what the basis for your questions is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to be specific. So the pathologist that works for the Defence team and that has the documentation that we have, he said that when preparing our reports he came across that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So now I'm asking you whether that could correspond to your own recollection in terms of the number of autopsy reports that bore your signature?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: You're asking a different question now. You're asking the ones I just did myself? Bore my signature? I can't -- I can't imagine that it was 2- or 300 cases in which all we had was forearm bone or a leg bone, et cetera. Perhaps your pathologist colleague is including the skull. Hopefully he will be including the skull as a single bone. So without checking actually my individual figures, I don't think I could agree with 2- or 300 cases in which all we looked at was just a single bone. I think there was usually more, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Professor. Then I'm just going to take an example. 1D01288. 1D01288.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, is that an example of a single bone? Because the witness has said that he vaguely thinks that there may have been 50 or 60. So unless there's any other reason why you want to present this to us, but the witness acknowledges that there were such cases. Again, I do not know what you're heading for, but if it is to establish that there were single bone case, there's no need to do that. Because you would have at least 50 or 60 most likely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The number may be higher but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's a matter of counting. Parties could sit together. Three thousand reports, just count the ones -- or if it's a strong -- if it is an important matter for the Defence, give us the numbers, and we'll have a look at -- because if your expert looked at it, Mr. Stojanovic, I take it that he has taken notes as to where to find the 300.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, Your Honour, and then we're going to proceed. However, on the basis of this example, I would like to put two additional questions about this entire line of questioning for the professor, with your leave, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so. If there's more than just establishing the other one -- the one-bone cases, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, let us accept that this would be one of those reports, if you agree. This is an analysis of practically one single bone, a right forearm bone, if I see it properly. And it is stated very correctly that no cause of death can be determined. However, I wanted to ask you something: On the basis of what you said in terms of how you worked at the Visoko mortuary, was this dealt with already in a number -- in another case that you were working on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this -- this examination dealt with ... I don't follow your question, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I shall rephrase. Maybe I made a mistake. This is Ravnice. We'll go back to that. Can you see that in the report - right? - so it's the Ravnice grave-site. Would it be right and possible in view of the methodology of your work at the mortuary that, under quotation marks, and sorry about that, the "owner" of this right forearm bone had already been registered under a different number, because that's where the complete body was, and that there are two numbers that actually pertain to one and the same body. In one case, it's just one bone; and, in another case, it's the entire body or a group of body parts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I thought that I had asked the same question already to Mr. Clark before and that he had answered that question. Unless you think that this is a question different from one of the questions I've put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I was going to say that, yes, it is perfectly true that we may have seen the rest of the body and given it a different number, yes. That's why -- that's why if my calculations I did not include the body parts. We always stuck to the bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you have the impression that you had answered the same question already before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I thought I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there's no need to put the same questions and hear the same answer, Mr. Stojanovic. Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the answers that you provided related to DNA analysis, do you know whether the bodies that were the subject of your expertise in 1999, whether they were buried before the Bosnian Commission was trained for DNA analysis?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: As I am aware, the bodies were not buried. I think they were stored, stored in Tuzla, and then DNA analysis was carried out. And once identification had been established, a positive identification, the bodies were then released for burial. But I'm not aware of any bodies being buried without identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And by "identification," you mean through DNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: DNA. A positive name put on DNA, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, in one of the answers you provided during the examination-in-chief, you mentioned ligatures that were found in some graves. And you said that that was Kozluk, Lazete, and, to the best of your recollection, one of the graves in Glogova.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Bodies from the grave in Nova Kasaba were also the subject of your analysis. And, if you remember, on two occasions, you analysed the bodies from these graves from Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us not open the document now. You can look at the summary of the findings for Nova Kasaba. But will we agree that in Nova Kasaba, because that is not in the summary, there was not a single body that was found with ligatures or blindfolds? That's page 16 of your report.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Well, one possible. One possible blindfold, but, yes. Nobody with any definite blindfold or ligature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, these 55 bodies found in a few graves, mostly in two, as you had said, you cannot actually establish the time of death of these persons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, likewise, on the basis of the rules of your profession - we are talking about Nova Kasaba now - you cannot establish the locations where these persons died? I'm talking again on the basis of the rules of your profession.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No. I should actually say yes there. Because you said "you cannot establish," so ... you know what I mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Thank you. Now you can follow. I am going to move on a bit faster. Konjevic Polje. The Konjevic Polje graves had also two sites, if you will, a total of 12 bodies. And, again, you said in the summary, page 19, Professor, so you can follow it in your report, you say that these bodies had no blindfolds or ligatures.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I'm asking myself for the last four, five questions, whether there's any dispute about these matters, if no ligatures are mentioned, whether the Prosecution, nevertheless would have some hidden ligatures somewhere. I mean, if the report doesn't say so, then it -- at least at the starting point for the Chamber to think about these matters would be that there were no ligatures reported here and, therefore, that the witness would not have found any ligatures because he would have reported about them, if he would have found them. That's -- that's my way of thinking, and I think I'm speaking on behalf of my colleagues as well. Apart from that, Ms. D'Ascoli, any dispute about these matters?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. We stand by what is in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, Mr. Stojanovic, to verify that everything which was not in the report was not a finding by the witness doesn't make much sense. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. With all due respect, I also took into account what Professor Baraybar said in relation to the ligatures. Thank you. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What Mr. Baraybar said is what Mr. Baraybar found. What this witness says is what he found. And there's no reason, I think, unless there's any specific question to put to this witness whether he has -- because that's the suggestion, he has left anything out of his report which seems to be of relevance where Mr. Baraybar would have perhaps taken a different position. I -- I reiterate that we should use our time as efficiently as possible. And, apart from that, there's no dispute about these matters. So ... Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, my next question: Konjevic Polje, according to the rules of your profession, you cannot establish the time of death for those 12 persons whose bodies are in these graves; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I cannot -- cannot establish the time of death, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask you, whether, in accordance with the rules of your profession as a pathologist, you allow for the possibility that these bodies had been transferred from somewhere and brought to that grave in Konjevic Polje, that the execution had not taken place at that particular location?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I -- I had assumed that that was entirely a possibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, may I have a minute of consultation with my client?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may consult with your client. Briefly and not audible for the other people in the courtroom. Please proceed. To consult.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, just one question. Let's go back to something. In view of your many years of experience and your work on these cases, on the basis of the samples that you had with regard to an entire body or a part of a body, on the basis of anthropological, morphological, or other qualities of the skeletal remains or soft tissue remains, could you establish what the race of a particular individual was?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Also I'd like to ask you, Professor, to look at page 24 of your report - we'll do this together - it contains the summary for Glogova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, there are many reports. To which report are you referring?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. For the transcript, P2259. We're still on that. 2259. Thank you for having cautioned me about this. So it's page 24. Could we please take a look at this together. Thank you. So we're looking at the last line.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is what I'd like to ask you, Professor, and during all these years that I have been working on this case, I could not establish this and I could not link all of this up: "Evidence of presumed post-mortem burning of many bodies, mostly the clothing, but, in several cases, involving the bones themselves." Now, this is what I'd like to ask you, Professor: On the basis of what is it being concluded that it's post-mortem, post-mortem burning of bodies or clothing, as you say here? I'm just speaking on the basis of the rules of your profession.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That -- that was an assumption. In my experience, for bone to be burned, the person is almost certainly dead. I mean, to get burning extending down through all the soft tissues to somebody's bone virtually always implied that the person is dead because it takes such a long time to do that. Additionally, we found -- the burning involved -- the broken -- the broken surface of the bones now. That would have only been broken at the time of death, so you were looking at fractures which had occurred at time of death which had also been burned with the implication that it must have occurred after death. But largely it was because it's -- it's almost inconceivable that somebody would still be alive in which the fire had got down to the surface of the bone and they weren't already dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I assume - and that is what your report says - that you were informed that Glogova is a primary grave?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that today as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I assume, Professor, that you know that Glogova 5 and Glogova 2 that you analysed had not been violated or attacked or looted earlier on as is stated in certain reports. Rather, these were intact graves that had been exhumed and opened?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. I understood that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Your two previous answers, would they lead to the conclusion that these bodies were burned post-mortem or partly burned post-mortem at some other place from where they were brought and buried in Glogova?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That -- that -- that would be my interpretation of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. That's what I wanted to hear about from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I need to deal with Ravnice, and I will require about 15 or 20 minutes for that. Thereby, I think that I will be within the confines of the time that I had envisaged. So perhaps it would be the right time to take the break and I have also discussed this with my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will take the break, but I have one question before we take the break. Being burned up to the bone level of bodies, I don't know whether I've missed something, but were these burned bodies next to not-burned bodies, or is there any possibility that they would have been burned together, already being in the grave? Or if you don't know ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't answer that specifically. I think it's possible that several bodies burned at the same time were close to each other, but -- and I'm sure that in the grave there were some non-burned bodies and some burned bodies. I can't answer that in any detail, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But you more or less agreed with the conclusion that the bodies would been burned and then taken to that grave which was not -- I'm wondering whether there was any possibility that the bodies were taken to the grave and then burned there, more of them. You would not expect just one isolated body to be burned, but if you burn in a grave with more bodies, then you would except other bodies to be affected by the fire as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My impression of the burning, rightly or wrongly, was that these -- this was not an attempt to get rid of bodies by burning. This was bodies which had been injured and which, subsequently, there was a fire beside them which caused localised burning of bones because it was not the whole body that was burnt, it was just maybe one part of it. And I got the impression that these were bodies very close to something which was burning and that caused burning of that bone. I didn't get the idea that these were -- this was a collection of bodies which had been put together and had been set alight to try and destroy them. That was not my impression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not collectively burned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. We'll take the break. Could the usher escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli, if I misspoke - there's a fair chance I did - in my reference to what appears in the transcript as page "12058 [sic]," it was "1258 [sic]." The date, 21st of August of last year, was accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: That's noted. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is 1200 -- when I said 58. I'm making another mistake. It was "12085." 12.000 -- that's the comedy of errors or the tragedy of errors. But it was "1285." I stop immediately because I did it right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a Monday, after all, Your Honours. Could we see P2260 in e-court, page 19 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, that's your summary report for Lazete, Glogova, and Ravnice, dated 22 February 2001. I have one question regarding -- this is page 19. Thank you. Can we proceed, Professor?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We are still discussing excavations at Glogova. In one of the graves you mentioned in the previous report, you say that you have established that the type of injuries on the mortal remains were blast injuries, which can happen when a shell or a rocket explodes. Such injuries, could they result from mines and explosives, such as a trip-wire or an anti-personnel mine?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, that would be possible. These are injuries caused by something exploding and parts of the casing striking the body. So whether that's a mine or some other explosive object, I -- I can't really say. The fact that we found pieces of, specific pieces of shrapnel, which were led to believe you could find in a grenade, led to us believe that at least some of these injuries were caused by grenades exploding.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the system where I come from, we usually ask questions about juxtaposition. Would the injured person, in view of the locality of these injuries, be standing, sitting, or perhaps crouching, or in another position?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I don't think I can say. It could have been any of these -- any of these positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now look at page 26 of the same report - for the record, it's P2260 - where you analyse body parts and bodies found at Ravnice. I have a few things to ask you about this grave. It's also in your own report, Professor. Tell me just that I'm right in thinking that it's a particular grave compared to all the others, because it includes body parts and bodies that were not buried, that were on the surface all the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, the report from 2001 is a better one to look at the Ravnice cases because it brings them all together. But, you're right, Ravnice was different. This was not a grave, as such. This was a grave-site, with bodies buried on the sur -- with bodies lying on the surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The fact that the bodies were on the surface would mean, if I understood your previous anticipate answers correctly, were subject to faster degradation; right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That's right, and they would also be subject to interference by animals who would be attacking the bodies and perhaps taking parts away from them, and the bodies would get scattered all the more, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And relative to the other grave-sites where you analysed the bodies at the mortuary, this grave contained the greatest number of body parts, as opposed to complete bodies, precisely for the reasons you just described?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That's right. I understood this -- Ravnice was on a slope so when a body begins to disintegrate, bones may roll down the slope. Animals almost certainly have come and taken a bone and removed it for another 50 feet away, et cetera. So, yes, that's why there were so many body, individual -- separate body parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: From what you analysed within your expertise, would it be correct to conclude that those bodies had been transported from somewhere and placed there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That was always my assumption that these bodies were -- were moved there to the top of the slope and probably just thrown over the slope.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The theory of our Defence is that those bodies had been collected along the route where the 28th Division had attempted to break through. I want to ask you whether you had any input information as to the distance at which this column moved, in which direction it moved, and where combat with this column took place?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: None at all. I have no information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that, relative to the other graves, that last parameter regardless of its accuracy concerning the number of shots that hit one body was slightly higher than the average in the case of Ravnice, unlike the other bodies in the graves?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. If I can just -- just refer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're consulting a report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm consulting my 2001 report which actually brings all the Ravnice cases together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the meantime can I ask a question, Mr. Stojanovic, I'm not quite sure I understand your question. What do you mean by "last parameter, regardless of its accuracy"?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at one point earlier today during the cross-examination, the professor told us that the information concerning the number of shots that hit one body is relative, because the whole body was not assembled so that the number of shots could have been higher if one or two shots were registered on separate body parts. That is page 27; P2261.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you be able to tell us now whether that would be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. We -- we worked out the average number of shots per person in Ravnice was four. Some people had been clearly shot just once. One man had been shot 14 times. But the overall average was about four shots. I think I understand what are you meaning, but because there are so many individual body parts here, that perhaps that average will -- will go up a bit. And, yes, I agree, that's -- that's entirely possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we have that on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then it's P2261, page 11 in English; and page 13 in B/C/S. P2261.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I should like to ask you to look at the same document, P2261, page 27, where we have a summary report concerning Zeleni Jadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's page 27 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: There it is, Professor. Page 31 in B/C/S. Concerning Zeleni Jadar. Just a few questions. This grave is the only atypical one that you performed your expertise on, and you were told it's a secondary grave; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you told that the bodies brought to the mortuary at Visoko where you were working from the sector of Zeleni Jadar originated from several secondary graves, not one?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No, well, we understood that this all came from one specific grave at Zeleni Jadar. I was aware that there were other graves at that site, but this -- this seemed to be all from one grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I also believe that it follows that they come from Zeleni Jadar 6, according to your report. I just wanted to ask you if there was intermingling of bodies from several graves named Zeleni Jadar. So your answer is no?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, according to the rules of your profession, as a pathologist, you are not able to say from where those bodies were brought into the secondary grave, Zeleni Jadar 6?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Generally, yes, that's the case, but there were some similarities between the bodies in Zeleni Jadar and some of those in Glogova. So I think in terms of shrapnel injuries. So, in that sense, we thought there must be a link -- well, it was likely there was a link between Glogova and this -- this grave, Zeleni Jadar 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But what I mean to say is, scientifically based on those similarities, could make a contention only between the body parts and bodies from Zeleni Jadar and Glogova because they have identical injuries, but the body parts and the complete bodies where there are no such injuries cannot be traced back to Zeleni Jadar. They could come from another locality; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes. Just for the record, you put Zeleni Jadar. It should be Glogova, I think. The very last ... You're right the bodies from Zeleni Jadar. Some could have come from Glogova; some could have come from elsewhere, yes. I can't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, thank you. These would be all our questions and bear with me for one more second. I want to see in my notes if I've missed something. Thank you, Professor, for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Ms. D'Ascoli, any further questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, just a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Clark, Mr. Stojanovic earlier on today asked you to confirm that, as a pathologist, you were not able to determine whether injuries were sustained before or after death. And you replied that yes, as you were dealing with, by and large, skeletons and bones that did not allow to say categorically that an injury occurred before or after death. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Now I understand there were exceptions to this. One of these being, for example, healing fractures whether -- well, on bones, whether ribs or skull, et cetera. So would healing fractures be a sign of injuries that occurred before the death.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 27400 on the screens. I'm just waiting for the document to appear. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sir, is this one of the autopsy reports that you performed at Kevljani?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you please comment on the summary of the autopsy report, in particular, the injuries.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: This was again a skeletonised body who had fractures in the skull and here we thought the fractures were such and where they were that almost certainly there must have been damage to the brain beneath. These were fractures at the back -- the back of the skull where the vital centres of brain lie underneath it. And I felt that -- and we also saw some blood clot beneath this, at the fractures. And I thought I justified here from my general pathology experience of saying that this -- that injury must have been what killed this man. In contrast to perhaps other cases in which there was a fracture of the skull perhaps on the top of the head which would not necessarily kill but something where this was and the type of fracture it was, and because there was blood clot underneath it, I felt I was on much safer ground on saying that this was the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: So, in this case blunt force injury to the head, also for the position was so severe to have caused the death of person.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, and this is based on my general pathology experience of knowing -- seeing people with injuries of that sort and realising that inevitably somebody with an injury like that is going to die.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions. The 65 ter 27400 is also in the document chart we discussed earlier so I don't need to tender it separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, there are some matters related to the exhibit and their admission but we can discuss it also without the witness.

utterances.text: Let me first see. Mr. Stojanovic, have the questions in re-examination triggered any need for further questions?

utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This then, Dr. Clark, concludes your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI

utterances.text: We have already --

utterances.text: We have already for the chart. Yes. And then 68 more. Nothing of those -- nothing is yet in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: No, none of them is in evidence and they can all be tendered as public exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I suggest that Mr. Registrar reserves 68 numbers for those and then prepares a list in which a number is assigned to each and every underlying document. Mr. Registrar, the numbers would be? The numbers to be reserved would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2270 onwards, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2270 onwards for 68. Well, then ... we -- we'll receive that list. Thank you very much. Is there any matter to be raised? We did understand that the next witness will be available tomorrow apart from whether it would be of any use to start any new testimony for the last five minutes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So after the videolink the other witness scheduled for Wednesday would be available.

utterances.text: Your Honour, actually, I still have the associated exhibits to the Krstic and Karadzic cases that needs to be dealt with. And there are 23.
